content: 1. Myocardial infarction, congestive cardiac failure, and/or episodes of coronary revascularization, bypass grafting, or angioplasty were included as composite cardiovascular disease outcomes in the studies reviewed. The quality of evidence supporting these findings was moderate. 2. A mean difference (MD) described as lower indicates a reduction in the outcome when comparing the group with increased potassium intake to the group with lower potassium intake. The quality of evidence for this finding was high. 3. No studies were identified that reported urinary catecholamine levels as an outcome. 4. The effect of increasing potassium intake to at least 90 mmol/day in adults (≥16 years of age) compared to lower intake was assessed. Data from cohort studies began with a GRADE of low quality, and some were downgraded further due to imprecision, as the 95% confidence intervals crossed the threshold of relevance for benefit or harm. 5. For coronary heart disease, no studies directly assessed the outcome, and no evidence was found to suggest a decreased risk with increased potassium intake. 6. Similarly, no studies directly assessed all-cause mortality as an outcome in relation to potassium intake. 7. Plasma noradrenaline levels were not directly assessed in any studies, and no evidence was available for this outcome. 8. Minor side effects were not reported in any of the studies reviewed. 9. Moderate-quality evidence suggests that increasing potassium intake is likely beneficial for blood pressure reduction, with the true effect being close to the estimate but with some possibility of variation. 10. Low-quality evidence indicates limited confidence in the effect estimate, and the true effect may differ substantially from the estimate. 11. Very low-quality evidence suggests minimal confidence in the effect estimate, with the true effect likely to differ significantly from the estimate. 12. One cohort observational study in children suggested a beneficial effect of increased potassium intake on blood pressure over time. 13. Data from adults were used as a proxy for children in some cases, as direct evidence in children was limited. 14. The potassium content of various food groups was approximated based on global food composition databases. For example, beans and peas contain approximately 1300 mg of potassium per 100 g, while fruits like bananas and papayas contain about 300 mg per 100 g. These values are for general comparison and not for estimating daily intake. 15. The WHO guideline on potassium intake for adults and children emphasizes the importance of increasing potassium consumption through dietary advice, specific foods, supplements, or whole diets, while avoiding confounding factors such as other dietary or lifestyle interventions. 16. The guideline also highlights the need for further research to determine the optimal level of potassium intake for maximum health benefits, particularly in children and adolescents. 17. High-quality evidence supports the beneficial effects of increased potassium intake on blood pressure in adults, with no indication of adverse effects. This relationship is indirectly linked to cardiovascular disease outcomes, such as stroke and coronary heart disease. 18. Limited direct evidence on cardiovascular disease and coronary heart disease outcomes shows no harm or benefit from increased potassium intake. 19. Low-quality direct evidence suggests a potential benefit of increased potassium intake on reducing cardiovascular disease risk, but further research is needed to confirm these findings.
